titulo.texto: Amate Paper Sheets and Ritual Figures from San Pablito Pahuatlán

frase_gancho.texto: Bark-paper cutouts where the spirits of maize and water live.

puente_narrativo.texto: From paper we move on to cloth. Look for a white huipil, almost transparent, made of fine cotton, embroidered with birds and flowers and accompanied by a red and green wool headdress.

guion_corto.texto: This paper is called amate, and it is made in San Pablito, an Otomí town in the highlands of Puebla. It is made from the bark of certain trees, which is boiled with lime or ash, laid out in strips on a board, and beaten with a stone until the fibers fuse into a single sheet. It is a very old technique. Here you will also see figures cut out of that paper. They represent spirits: of maize, of water, of the hills, and also of illnesses. Ritual specialists use them in ceremonies called “the custom,” to heal, to ask for rain, and to bless the harvests. The paper is not just a material: it is a way of speaking with the spirits.

guion_largo.texto:
The paper you use every day is a recent invention compared with amate. Long before the Spaniards, the peoples of Mexico were already making paper from the bark of trees such as the jonote and the fig. The Mexica received thousands of sheets as tribute from the peoples they dominated, and the codices of ancient Mexico were painted on amate or on deerskin.

The word “amate” comes from the Nahuatl amatl, which simply means “paper”; so when we say “amate paper” we are really saying “paper paper.” See how it is made. First the bark is cut and boiled for hours with lime or ash to soften it. Then the strips are laid out on a board, one beside another, in a grid pattern, and beaten with a grooved stone. The blows fuse the fibers, and as it dries it becomes a sturdy sheet, brown or cream in color. The whole process is done by hand, and it takes hours.

Amate paper had a bad reputation. The Spanish clergy associated it with forbidden rites and tried to put an end to its use. It is thought that in remote places like San Pablito the tradition survived thanks to the isolation of the highlands and the strength of ritual practices. It is a story of quiet resistance.

And here comes the heart of the matter. In San Pablito, ritual specialists cut the paper to make figures of spirits: of maize, of water, of the wilderness, of lightning, and also of illnesses. The figures receive offerings, are placed on altars, and, when the ceremony ends, are given back to the earth. This practice is called the custom, and it is used to heal, to ask for rain, and to bless the harvests.

Color matters. It is said that light paper is used for benevolent spirits and dark paper for the spirits of the night and of illnesses. So, with just two shades of paper and a pair of scissors, an entire universe is created. Each cutout is unique, and whoever makes it has known the rules since childhood.

There is one more story. In the 1960s, Nahua artisans from Guerrero began to paint on this paper, in vivid colors, scenes from the life of their communities, and so a new art was born. You will see examples in the Nahua Peoples Hall. In this way, a ritual paper ended up becoming a canvas, and today it is sold in markets all over the country. The old and the new joined hands.

San Pablito is now a town famous for its paper: almost every family makes it, and it is used for painting, for notebooks, for lamps, and for decoration. That industry has given work to many people, although it requires taking care of the trees that provide the bark.

When you see the silhouettes, remember that they are not dolls. They are beings with names, with powers, and with needs. For the person who cuts them, they speak, they listen, and they can help. The museum shows them in a display case, but their original place is an altar surrounded by flowers and candles.

texto.Region: Sierra Norte de Puebla (San Pablito Pahuatlán)
texto.Technique/Material: Jonote bark, boiled, macerated and boiled, with a striated river stone
texto.Function: Sacred medium for shamanic healing rites, spiritual cleansings and traditional craft

texto.pregunta: Myth: Amate paper is a modern craft made to sell to tourists.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a technology more than a thousand years old. In San Pablito it is still used in healing rituals and rituals to ask for rain.
